chunks: "The gate of a MOSFET is basically a capacitor: a metal or polysilicon plate, a very thin layer of silicon dioxide, and the silicon underneath.
That oxide is only a few nanometers thick in a logic transistor, and maybe tens of nanometers to around a hundred in a power MOSFET.

Silicon dioxide can only withstand an electric field of roughly 10 megavolts per centimeter, and the field is just the voltage over the thickness, so a few volts across a few nanometers is already close to the limit.
If you exceed it, the oxide breaks down and the gate shorts to the channel, permanently.
That's why the abs-max V GS on a power FET is often only about ±20 volts, and on a logic-level one ±8 to ±12 volts.
It's also unforgiving because the gate has no DC path and tiny capacitance.
A little static charge, say a nanocoulomb from a fingertip, on a few-picofarad gate gives hundreds of volts.
And in a circuit, the gate drive loop has inductance, so it rings and overshoots the drive voltage, and a fast drain edge couples a spike back through the Miller capacitance.
So I'd protect the gate with a series resistor to damp ringing, a Zener or TVS across gate and source to clamp, a pull-down resistor so it never floats, and ESD diodes at chip inputs."
